assurance.title: Can a command be forged, altered or replayed?
assurance.body:
The broker is not trusted. Its credentials are shared, so assume anyone
can read every topic and publish to every topic. What stops them is
checked on the repeater, and only there.

On lou-20 and later
  A command is sealed to one node and signed inside. The signature
  covers the node's own key, the road (MQTT or mesh), the counter, the
  expiry, the reply id and the command, so a command for one node
  verifies on no other, and one sent over MQTT is never taken as a mesh
  one. Commands and answers are encrypted between the node and you: the
  broker reads none of it and cannot tell which nodes are yours. There
  is no broadcast topic. The counter and the expiry work as below. What
  follows describes the old scheme of lou-19 and older, which a lou-20
  node with an IATA code also accepts until lou-21.

What the signature covers
  The repeater verifies an Ed25519 signature over the topic, a newline,
  and "v1|counter|expiry|command". Every byte of that is covered, so a
  changed counter, a longer expiry, a different command, a touched
  signature, or the same payload on another node's topic, another
  region's topic or the broadcast topic all fail with sig-invalid. Only
  the one public key the repeater was given (see [[signing]])
  verifies; the key on this machine never leaves it inside anything but
  a signature.

Why the counter stops a replay
  A repeater stores the counter of every command it accepts, before it
  runs the command, and refuses any counter that is not greater than the
  stored one. The same envelope published again -- a minute later or a
  month later, by you or by anyone -- is refused as replay. The store
  survives a reboot. mccontrol uses unix seconds as the counter, so a
  new command always carries a higher one.

Why the expiry matters as well
  A captured envelope the repeater has not seen yet could be held and
  published later. The expiry limits that to the envelope's life (five
  minutes by default, an hour at most; the repeater refuses anything
  further off than that), and the counter still lets it run once at
  most. The same holds for a broadcast: a repeater that was offline
  when it was sent will accept it once if it is republished within its
  life, which is what you asked for anyway. A repeater with no clock
  refuses rather than guesses.

What this does not give you
  Secrecy, on lou-19 and older: commands and replies are readable by
  anyone on the broker (from ar-13 a command to a node whose whole key
  is known goes encrypted). Nothing secret travels in a command; the
  settings that would be (the signing key, the identity key, erase)
  are not admitted at all.
  Delivery: the broker can drop or delay a command. That shows as
  silence or as expired, never as a wrong command running.
  Trustworthy results from older firmware: up to ar-10 a result line
  is not signed, so anyone on the broker can publish "ok" in such a
  repeater's name. From ar-11 the node signs every result with its own
  key and the tool checks it: a result marked [signed] is the node's
  word, a BAD SIGNATURE line is a forgery and is ignored, and an
  unmarked line is an r1 from older firmware -- confirm those with a
  read whose answer you can judge.
  A stolen key: whoever reads key.seed can sign as you. It is kept
  readable only by you. From lou-20, rotate it with rekey before the
  thief does (python -m mccontrol.rekey, see [[signing]]): whoever holds
  a node's command key can replace it first, and then only a serial
  visit gets the node back. On lou-19 and older, replacing the key
  silences every repeater until each is re-provisioned over serial.

How this is checked
  tests/test_envelope.py builds envelopes and judges them the way the
  firmware does, in the same order: signature, counter, expiry. Each
  property above has a test that goes red if the rule is loosened.

See [[signing]], [[protocol]] and [[broker]].

broker.title: The control broker
broker.body:
Commands and results travel through an MQTT broker, the one each
repeater's cmd.slot points at. Nodes on lou-20 or later all use the
shared broker, with no region. For lou-19 and older the shared broker
serves every region; a region may run its own, and then the configuration names it
for that region ("mccontrol config --region-broker VGR=<host>"). Each
device is reached through its region's broker, and each device shows
which one. The configuration also holds the port, username, password
and how long to wait for answers, the same for every broker. Your key is
registered once per broker. [[ownregion]] has the steps. The broker
test connects with those, subscribes to a test topic, publishes to it
and checks the broker delivers it back; each step is reported and the
first failure named ("Not authorized" is the broker rejecting the
username or password). "mccontrol config" and "mccontrol test" do the
same ("mccontrol test --region VGR" tests a region's own broker); where
they are in your interface is in [[keys]].

This is not the broker the repeaters' statistics go to; those credentials
are not used here.

Back to [[index]].

Signing in. With no username set, the tool signs in to the broker the
way a node does: the username is "v1_" plus your public key and the
password a token signed by your key, renewed each session -- nothing to
hand out, nothing to type. That is how the default broker,
mqtt-meshcore.louie.se, knows who is publishing. A login from the broker's
password file sets its username and password here, and then those are
used.

cautions.title: Commands that take something away
cautions.body:
These are sent only after you have been told what they do and have
said to send them anyway:

  region denyf *       stops the repeater forwarding every unscoped
                       message. It may be the only link between two
                       places that rely on that.
  region denyf <name>  stops forwarding that scope.
  region remove <name> deletes the region; messages scoped to it drop.
  set autoreply off    stops answering test requests.
  reboot, clkreboot    restarts the node: off the air and off the control
                       plane until it is back.
  set mqtt.iata        moves the node to another region's topics. On
                       lou-19 and older, change its region here to
                       match; a lou-20 node is reached without it.
  set mqttN.*          changes that slot's broker or credentials; if the
                       control plane rides that slot, it may go silent.
  set name             renames the node as the whole mesh sees it.

set repeat off, erase and set cmd* are not cautions any more: the
firmware refuses them outright, and so does this tool, before signing
(see [[commands]]).

One of these sent to a region or a county goes to every node of yours
there and cannot be undone in one step. The node does not second-guess
a signed command; this question is where it is asked.
See [[send]].

cli.title: The command line
cli.body:
The same work without the screens:

  mccontrol keygen                      create the signing key
  mccontrol key                         print the public key
  mccontrol config --username u --password p [--broker h --port n]
  mccontrol test                        test the control broker
  mccontrol discover [--add]            your lou-20 nodes, from their alive
  mccontrol discover JKG [--add]        lou-19 and older, by region
  mccontrol add <name> <64-hex key>     by its whole key, no region (lou-20)
  mccontrol add <name> <8-hex node> <region> [notes]     (lou-19 and older)
  mccontrol devices                     list your devices
  mccontrol send loutest region put se-jkp '*'
  mccontrol send JKG region allowf se-jkp --all    each of your nodes in JKG
  mccontrol send se-jkp ver --county    each node with that region home
  mccontrol send loutest region --dry-run     sign and print, send nothing
  mccontrol regions loutest             read the map
  mccontrol group create canary loutest gisebo   a named group of devices
  mccontrol group add|remove canary <device...>
  mccontrol group send canary ver       each member in turn, its own topic
  mccontrol groups                      the groups and their members
  mccontrol history loutest             each line says its road (mqtt, mesh, relay)
  mccontrol config --companion tcp:10.0.0.5:5000   your radio, for the mesh
  mccontrol send loutest ver --via mesh       through your companion
  mccontrol send loutest ver --via auto       the mesh when MQTT has failed
  mccontrol send cabin ver --via relay:loutest    loutest sends it by radio
  mccontrol send cabin ver --via relay:loutest --route flood
  mccontrol send cabin time now --via relay:loutest    mend its clock
  python -m mccontrol.rekey start|send|status|finish   a new key, no visit
  mccontrol help [topic]                this help as text

A device is named by its name or by any unique prefix of its name or id.
Commands that take something away ask on the command line too; --yes
skips the question. The roads are in [[mesh]] and [[relay]], the key
rotation in [[signing]]. Back to [[index]].

commandlist.title: The command list
commandlist.body:
Every command the control plane admits, by group: reads, auto-reply,
regions, tuning, MQTT, node, for the tagged devices, or the current one
when none is tagged. Typing narrows the list.

What choosing a command does depends on what it needs:

  nothing       it runs at once, and the reply is shown when it arrives
                (ver, region, reboot)
  one value     one of its choices is picked, then it runs
                (set autoreply on|off, set autoreply.mode ...)
  several       several of its choices are picked
  free text     a value is typed, with examples beside it (region put
                se-jkp *, set txdelay 0.5); an empty value asks again

Grey entries are commands the device's firmware does not admit: they
cannot be chosen, and the list says how many there are, what the device
reports (ar-10, or "unknown", which counts as the oldest) and that
reading names and versions fills it in. The fleet runs several firmware
versions for months, so this is how a command slot is never spent on a
not-allowed. ar-10, the oldest build the list knows, admits the auto-reply
settings, the two triggers and a dozen reads; ar-11 admits everything
on the deny list's far side (ver, get name, get stats, the region map,
the tuning writes, reboot...); lou-20 adds get sensors, get relay and
set relay. To make the grey go away, flash.

The list does not hold every setting. One that is not in it is typed
as a "set" or "get" with its name: set alive.interval 30, set
autoreply.national off, get cmd.mesh. [[commands]] names the ones that
came with lou-20.

From lou-14 a version also says which features the image was built
with (ar auto-reply, rc this command plane): esp32s3-v1.17.1-lou-14-arrc-
.... A command of a feature the image does not have is not greyed but
left out: an rc image without auto-reply has no trigger test, trigger
private or autoreply settings, and no build will give it them.

A command that takes something away still asks first (see [[cautions]]),
and one the firmware would refuse is stopped before it is signed, with
the reason (see [[commands]]).

The full table, with each command's kind, is "mccontrol commands".

See [[send]], [[reads]] and [[keys]].

commands.title: Commands a repeater admits over the control plane
commands.body:
Since the firmware of 2026-10-08 the control plane is a command centre:
every command the repeater's own console answers travels this way,
EXCEPT a deny list. A command must start with one of the verbs

  set  get  region  trigger test  trigger private  neighbor.remove
  sensor  gps  powersaving  clock          (with their arguments)
  ver  reboot  clkreboot  neighbors  board  memory  clear stats  ota check
  ota update  cmd ping  rekey <key>

and must match nothing on the deny list. This tool knows the list and
says why before signing, so a refused command costs no command slot:

  identity        set prv.key, set public.key
  the plane       set cmd (.slot, .pubkey), get cmd.pubkey
  credentials     password, wifi.pwd, wifi.ssid, guest.password,
                  alert.psk, bridge.secret, snmp.community, mqtt.email,
                  mqtt.owner, owner.info, tls*, get prv*, and a slot's
                  get mqttN.password / .token / .username
  destructive     erase, start *, poweroff, shutdown,
                  set bootloader.ver          (ota update is fine from lou-19,
                                              to one node at a time)
  position, role  set/get lat, set/get lon, set role, set repeat
  the radio       set freq, set radio*, set tx, set extra.sf,
                  set dutycycle, tempradio
  transmissions   advert*, alert *, set advert.interval,
                  set flood.advert.interval   (trigger is the one sanctioned transmit)
  the clock       time <epoch>                (clock sync is fine; over the
                                              mesh "time" is admitted)
  serial-only     log, stats-*

"set cmd" and "get cmd.pubkey" are the names on lou-20; on lou-19 and
older the same settings are "mqtt.cmd", denied in the same way (see
[[lou20]]). Over the mesh, and only there, the repair is admitted too:
set wifi.ssid, set wifi.pwd, set cmd on [<host>] and "time" (see
[[mesh]]).

What that leaves is most of what you want: every tuning setting
(txdelay, rxdelay, af, cad, int.thresh, flood.max, path.hash.mode,
loop.detect, ...), every mqtt.* and mqttN.* setting so a broker can be
replaced without a visit, set name, set relay, the auto-reply family,
the region map, reboot, and every read that names no secret.

The ones used most:

  region                   read the region map (the tree with F flags)
  region put <name> [*]    add a region as a child of * (or of a parent)
  region allowf <name>     forward floods carrying that scope
  region denyf <name>      stop forwarding that scope   (see [[cautions]])
  region remove <name>     delete a region             (see [[cautions]])
  region default <name>    the scope on the repeater's own adverts
  region save              keep the map after a reboot
  set autoreply on|off     answer test requests, or not
  set autoreply.<x> <v>    hops, direct.flood, slot, window, slots,
                           region, mode, private, national
  get autoreply[.<x>]      read them back
  trigger test [<id>] [F|P|D|S]      originate a test probe
  trigger private <64hex> [<id>]     a test request to one repeater
  ver / get name / neighbors / get radio / get repeat / reboot

New with lou-20 (a setting not in the command list is typed as a "set"
or "get" with its name):

  get cmd                  the plane's state on the node: on or "mesh
                           only", the counter, the slot, the last
                           command, and for the mesh road how many
                           requests were answered and refused
  get sensors              what the node measures, on either road:
                           > batt=3881mV mcu=21.5C temp=23.5C hum=40.5%
  get relay, set relay off|own
                           whether the node relays your commands, and
                           what is left of its budget (see [[relay]])
  set alive.interval <5-1440>
                           minutes between a node's alive messages,
                           default 15 (see [[discover]])
  set autoreply.national auto|off|<region>
                           the node also answers "test" on the national
                           test channel (#test-se in Sweden). auto, the
                           default, finds the country in the node's
                           region table; off stops it; a region name,
                           which must be in the table, sets it by hand.
                           "get autoreply.national" shows what it comes
                           to. Replies there cost the whole country
                           airtime: send one test, wait two minutes, do
                           not repeat it.
  get cmd.mesh             when the mesh road is open: off, on or auto
                           (see [[mesh]])
  rekey <new public key>   replace the command key without a visit;
                           "python -m mccontrol.rekey" does it for you
                           (see [[signing]])
  time now                 over the mesh only: mend a clock that fell
                           behind (see [[mesh]])

On the node's console only, never over the plane:

  set cmd.debug on|off     prints one line, "mcc: ...", for each command
                           or relayed request the node hears and where
                           it stopped: not listening, refused and why,
                           run, answered, the airtime sent. No key and
                           no command text. Until the next restart. The
                           relay's and the target's lines carry the
                           request's counter, so one command can be
                           followed across both. "get cmd.debug" says
                           which.
  set cmd.pubkey, set cmd on, set cmd.slot, set cmd.mesh
                           the plane's own settings (see [[signing]]).
                           cmd.mesh also from an admin login, and
                           "set cmd on" over the mesh as a repair.

Limits a node keeps, also for validly signed commands
  50 commands an hour per node (10 before lou-20), on every road. The
  hour slides: no span of 60 minutes holds more. Over it the node
  answers rate-limited; a refused command spends nothing.
  2 transmits an hour per node (trigger), counted apart.
  Over the mesh, an airtime budget for the answers (see [[mesh]]).
  A relay keeps a budget of its own (see [[relay]]).
  Password logins to a node (admin or guest, over the mesh) are
  throttled from lou-20: 5 wrong passwords and that sender is refused
  for 10 minutes. This tool never logs in with a password; the limit
  matters when you give a node its first key as an admin.

A region tree line with "|" (region def a|* b|*) cannot travel: "|" is the
envelope's field separator. Add names one at a time with region put.

"trigger" commands transmit on the air and go to one device only, never
to a region. In an rc image without auto-reply the triggers and the
autoreply settings are refused as not-allowed.
trigger private is answered only when the asking node and the target speak
the same private-test sub-type: 0x04 up to ar-13, 0xF0 from lou-14, with
no overlap. When both versions are known and differ, the tool says before
the results that no answer will come; flash the older one.
A node on the old ar-10 firmware admits only the
auto-reply family, the triggers and a dozen reads, and answers
not-allowed to the rest; the command list greys those out for it (see
[[commandlist]]), and "mccontrol commands <device>" marks them. A
not-allowed from a node whose firmware should admit the command is
said as a finding: the tool's table or the device's version is wrong.

devices.title: Devices
devices.body:
A device is a repeater you manage: a name you choose, its node id (the
first eight hex characters of its public key, which is how the firmware
names it on the control topics), for lou-19 and older the region its
observers use (the IATA code, such as JKG), and notes.

A device's name, region and notes can be edited. A device can be
forgotten after a confirmation; its history file stays on disk. Devices
are added by [[discover]] or by hand on the command line (see [[cli]]).

A node on lou-20 or later needs no region: it is reached by its whole
key alone, wherever it is. A device on lou-19 or older is reached
through its region; with none it cannot be sent to, so give it one.

A node without Wi-Fi (mesh only) is never found by a discovery. Add it
by its whole public key, with no region: "mccontrol add <name> <64
hex>". [[meshonly]] has the steps.

Back to [[index]].

Names and versions from the fleet. Reading names and versions sends "get
name" and "ver" to the tagged devices, or the current one: a device you
have not named takes the name the node answers with, a name you gave is
kept, and every device stores its firmware version, shown short in the
Ver column (ar-10 1.17.1) and sortable. Two signed reads per device,
each one of the node's command slots this hour; more than three devices
asks first. Firmware that admits neither read answers not-allowed and
the device keeps what it had. "mccontrol refresh" does the same from the
command line.

The whole key. A node on the firmware of 2026-10-08 or later (ar-11)
listens on a topic named by its whole 64-character key; older firmware
by the first 8. The tool keeps the whole key on the device when it
knows it -- a discovery sees it on the node's answer, and "mccontrol add
<name> <64 hex>" stores it -- and addresses each node by the
form its firmware uses. The 8-character id stays the name you see.

dialogs.title: Questions
dialogs.body:
A verb that needs values asks for them -- the one or two it needs, such
as a region, a command, a name -- and sends nothing until you answer.
Backing out of the question sends nothing. Earlier commands can be
recalled where a command is typed.

A question about a command that takes something away from a repeater
says so, and answering it is the only way that command is sent. See
[[cautions]].

Back to [[index]].

discover.title: Discovering repeaters
discover.body:
Nodes on lou-20 or later are found from their alive messages: each keeps
a sealed message on the broker that only its owner's key opens. A
discovery reads them all, sends nothing, asks for no region, and lists
the nodes that are yours wherever they are: online, offline, or no longer
yours (given another key). Found nodes are added with no region; they
need none. "mccontrol discover" (no region) does this on the command
line, "--add" keeps what it finds; each interface's discover key does the
same ([[keys]]).

An Observer node with a command key publishes its alive message soon
after it connects, then about every 15 minutes, so a node you have just
set up appears by itself within a few minutes. It carries the node's
version, region home, name, uptime, clock and how the plane is set.
"set alive.interval <5-1440>" changes the minutes between them and
travels over the plane; "get alive.interval" reads it. The broker clears
the message when the node drops off, which is what "offline" means. After
a network drop a node is back after about 3 minutes.

A mesh-only node, one without Wi-Fi, is never discovered: it has no MQTT
and sends no alive message. Add it by its public key; see [[meshonly]].
A node without a command key sends none either.

Nodes on lou-19 or older publish no alive message and are found by
region, the only place a region is still asked for: "mccontrol discover
<region>", or the interfaces' "discover a region (lou-19 and older)". It
sends one harmless read ("get autoreply"), signed with your key, to that
region's broadcast topic, and listens for answers. Only a node that
verified your signature publishes a result, so every node in the list is
yours; a node with another key, or none, says nothing. Several regions go
in one run -- "JKG, GOT" -- and "*" asks every region your directory
spans, one signed read per region.

The found nodes are listed with what each answered and "= name" where it
is already in your directory. Any of them, or all, are added to the
directory; a node the fleet gave no name is asked for one, or added
unnamed, to be named later. A node found by its alive gives its own name.

On lou-19 and older, a second read, "get name", fills in names on
firmware that admits it; older firmware refuses it and those nodes stay
unnamed.

Related: [[devices]], [[signing]], [[lou20]].

history.title: History
history.body:
Every command sent to a device is kept with what came back: the time, the
command, the topic, the result code in words and the reply. A device's
history is shown newest first, and any line opens the whole reply.

Whether the node signed the reply is kept too: a reply whose signature
failed is shown as "BAD SIGNATURE <reply>" and teaches nothing; one from
firmware that does not sign (older than ar-11) is shown "(unsigned)".

A command sent through a relay is kept with the relay, the route, how it
was sent and how well the relay heard the answer.

A send to a region is kept once per device, each with its own line, and
once for the region with how many answered.

The files are under your configuration directory, history/<node>.jsonl,
one line of JSON per command. See [[cli]] for "mccontrol history".

index.title: Help: contents
index.body:
mccontrol signs commands with your key and sends them to the repeaters you
run, over the control broker. Each interface has help of its own; these
are the texts every one of them shares, and what "mccontrol help" prints.

Getting around
  [[screen]]      what an interface shows: the directory, history, answers
  [[keys]]        the keys, and where each verb is
  [[dialogs]]     how a verb asks for its values

Doing things
  [[commandlist]] every command for a device, its parameter asked for
  [[send]]        send a command to one device, the tagged ones, or a region
  [[shortcuts]]   a command per slot, no question asked
  [[sets]]        command sets: a rollout as one named list of steps
  [[discover]]    find the repeaters that accept your key
  [[devices]]     add, edit, forget; names and regions
  [[history]]     what was sent and what came back
  [[mesh]]        repair a node over the mesh when its Wi-Fi or MQTT fails;
                why a command over the mesh gets no answer
  [[relay]]       a node of yours on MQTT sends the command by radio
  [[meshonly]]    set up and reach a node without Wi-Fi
  [[reads]]       last answers: what the device last answered to each read
  [[stats]]       a device's statistics: battery, airtime, noise floor, from Beacon

Reference
  [[lou20]]       firmware lou-20: the new names, upgrading, what is new
  [[commands]]    the commands a repeater admits over the control plane,
                and the limits it keeps
  [[cautions]]    the commands that take something away
  [[signing]]     your key, provisioning a repeater, replacing the key (rekey)
  [[assurance]]   can a command be forged, altered or replayed? what is not covered
  [[broker]]      the control broker, its credentials, the connection test
  [[ownregion]]   your own region: the shared broker or the region's own
  [[protocol]]    the envelope on the wire, for the curious
  [[cli]]         the same work from the command line

keys.title: Keys
keys.body:
Each interface has keys of its own, and its help lists them under this
topic: "mccontrol --ui <name>", then its help. Plain "mccontrol" starts
the last one asked for, or Monolith when none has been or the one kept
is gone. Every verb is also on the command line, one subcommand each;
see [[cli]].

Discovery asks for no region: it reads the alive messages of your
lou-20 and later nodes, wherever they are, and each interface's help
names the key that starts it. Only lou-19 and older nodes are found by
region, through a discovery of their own ("discover <region>" on the
command line). See [[discover]].

Back to [[index]].

lou20.title: lou-20: what changed, and upgrading
lou20.body:
Firmware lou-20 (v1.18.0-lou-20) changed how a node is reached and what
its settings are called. This tool speaks both the new scheme and the
old one, and picks per node by the node's version.

The settings have new names
  Remote control works without Wi-Fi or MQTT now, so its settings are
  no longer called mqtt.cmd. On lou-20 the old names are gone: the node
  answers them as unknown.

    lou-19 and older            lou-20
    set mqtt.cmd on [<host>]    set cmd on [<host>]
    set mqtt.cmd off            set cmd off
    get mqtt.cmd                get cmd
    set mqtt.cmd.pubkey <key>   set cmd.pubkey <key>
    get mqtt.cmd.pubkey         get cmd.pubkey
    set mqtt.cmd.slot <n>       set cmd.slot <n>
    mqtt.cmd ping               cmd ping

  Relaying is "set relay off|own", outside cmd. A node on lou-19 or
  older knows only the old names: type those there.

Upgrading a node
  The settings carry over: the command key, its counter and the slot.
  Only what you type has changed. Nothing needs to be set again, with
  one exception: a lou-18 node set with "set mqtt.cmd on <host>" lost
  that slot at its next reboot (a fault in lou-18). Type "set cmd on
  <host>" once more after the upgrade to stay on that server, or the
  bare "set cmd on" for the shared broker, which is where this tool
  reaches a lou-20 node (see [[ownregion]]).
  A lou-19 Observer node takes "ota update" over the old scheme, comes
  back on lou-20, and the tool moves to the new scheme at its first
  alive message. Rolling back to lou-18 keeps the key, counter and slot.

The old scheme stays until lou-21
  A lou-20 node with an IATA code (mqtt.iata) still accepts everything
  lou-18 did, on meshcore/<IATA>/<key>/cmd. lou-21 removes that. The
  tool sends the new scheme to a node whose alive message opened with
  your key or whose version is lou-20 or later, and the old one to
  every other node, on its stored region. The device view says which.

Gone already
  A command to a whole region at once. A send to a region or a county
  is now one command per node, spaced apart (see [[send]]).

New in lou-20, and where it is explained
  No region          a node is reached by its key alone and needs no
                     IATA code. See [[devices]] and [[protocol]].
  Alive messages     your Observer nodes appear by themselves. See
                     [[discover]].
  Mesh-only nodes    remote control on boards without Wi-Fi. See
                     [[meshonly]].
  The relay          a node on MQTT sends your command by radio. See
                     [[relay]].
  Over the mesh      repair, silence and answers, "time now". See
                     [[mesh]].
  rekey              a new command key without a visit, and the first
                     key from an admin login. See [[signing]].
  New commands       get sensors, set alive.interval, set
                     autoreply.national, cmd.debug, and the limits (50
                     commands an hour). See [[commands]].

Related: [[index]], [[ownregion]].

mesh.title: Repair a node over the mesh
mesh.body:
When a repeater's Wi-Fi or MQTT fails -- a new Wi-Fi password, a moved
access point, a renamed broker -- it drops off the control plane, but its
radio is still on the mesh. From lou-19 a node with the plane (rc) also
takes your signed commands as a LoRa request, sent through your own
companion radio or, from lou-20, through a relay (see [[relay]]). Same
key, same signature, same counter: a command delivered both ways runs
once. The answer comes back over the air. A node without Wi-Fi is
reached this way always; see [[meshonly]].

Switch on while it works
  The node's mesh road is the setting cmd.mesh: auto (the default)
  opens it once MQTT has been down 15 minutes; on keeps it open; off
  shuts it. Check it now, while MQTT works: send "get cmd.mesh".
  "set cmd.mesh off|on|auto" is typed on the node's console or from an
  admin login; it does not travel over the plane. A device group (see
  [[cli]]) reads it from every node in one go.
  Make sure each device has its whole public key (discovery stores it):
  the request is encrypted to that key.
  Set your companion once:
    mccontrol config --companion tcp:10.0.0.5:5000
    (or serial:/dev/ttyACM0, or ble:AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF)
  A tcp: companion runs the Wi-Fi companion firmware, which listens on
  port 5000 and serves one client: each mesh command drops whatever held
  it (the phone app). To share it, put a mux in front and give mccontrol
  the mux's port (tcp:<host>:5001). The web app reaches it through
  mccontrol-bridge, or connects a companion by USB or Bluetooth.

The recipe
  1. Connect your companion, in reach of the node or of the mesh. Or
     name a relay: --via relay:<device> in place of --via mesh.
  2. Send the repair over the mesh:
       mccontrol send loutest set wifi.ssid HomeNet --via mesh
       mccontrol send loutest set wifi.pwd s3cret --via mesh
     or point the command slot at the broker:
       mccontrol send loutest set cmd on --via mesh
       mccontrol send loutest set cmd on mqtt.example.se --via mesh
     The bare "set cmd on" puts the slot back on the shared broker.
     (On lou-19 the line is "set mqtt.cmd on".)
  3. Reboot to apply it:  mccontrol send loutest reboot --via mesh
     A reboot answers nothing; the node restarts first.
  4. Confirm on MQTT, a few minutes later:  mccontrol send loutest ver
     A node is back on the plane about 3 minutes after its network is.

What the mesh road admits
  Everything the plane admits over MQTT, and only here the repair:
  set wifi.ssid, set wifi.pwd (each with a value), set cmd on and
  set cmd on <host>, and "time" (below). The broker slots' settings
  (set mqttN.*) travel too, so a broken Observer feed can be repaired
  over the mesh as well. Everything else denied stays denied. A command
  is at most 57 bytes to a node on lou-20 or later (sealed) and 59 to
  one on lou-19, checked before it is signed. One node at a time,
  never a region. 50 commands an hour on every road.

Flood and direct
  A request goes direct, along a known path, or as a flood, which every
  repeater in reach repeats. The first request to a node with no known
  path floods once. A node answers a flooded request 15 to 30 seconds
  after it arrives, so that the answer does not collide with the copies
  of the request. A request that came direct is answered at once.
  The flooded answer teaches the way back: your companion (or the
  relay) learns the path and sends it to the node, and the next
  requests and answers go direct, as a few packets and no flood.
  A path that has stopped working shows as no answer to a direct
  command. One flooded command renews it.

No answer
  Over the mesh, silence is not a refusal. It is one of two things.
  The packet was lost: the request on the way out, or the answer on
  the way back. If the answer was lost, the command may have run. Read
  the setting back before you send a change again.
  The node did not answer on purpose. It says nothing at all when:
    its answer airtime is used up. A node answers on a budget of its
    own: 5 % of 15 minutes (45 s on the air), then 1 % of the next 15
    (9 s), then a burst again. Wait a few minutes and send it again.
    the request was not signed by its command key, or its counter was
    not new (a replay).
    its firmware is older than lou-19, or has no remote control.
  Tell them apart with "get cmd": its line ends ", mesh <mode> ok <n>
  refused <n>". A request over the budget is counted under refused; a
  lost packet is counted nowhere.
  mesh-closed is an answer, not silence: the node's MQTT works, so it
  takes commands over MQTT. Send it there.

A clock that fell behind: time now
  A node without Wi-Fi has no time source. One whose clock was set once
  and has fallen behind refuses every command as expiry-too-far. Send
    mccontrol send cabin time now --via mesh
  (or --via relay:<device>). The tool sends this computer's time as
  "time <epoch>". It is admitted over the mesh only, never over MQTT,
  on lou-20 or later, and at most an hour ahead of the sender's clock.
  It only moves a clock forward: a clock that is ahead needs a visit.
  A clock still at the firmware's default needs nothing: the node skips
  the expiry check until its clock is set.

--via auto
  Takes the mesh for a mesh-only node, for a command only the mesh
  admits, for a node whose status Beacon has not seen for 15 minutes
  (mccontrol config --mesh-after-mins), or when the broker cannot be
  reached; otherwise MQTT. A mesh-closed answer is sent again over MQTT.
  History says which road each command took.

Related: [[relay]], [[meshonly]], [[send]], [[signing]], [[history]].

meshonly.title: A node without Wi-Fi (mesh only)
meshonly.body:
From lou-20 remote control also works on boards without Wi-Fi: the rc
and arrc images for stock MeshCore boards (nRF52, RP2040, STM32, and an
ESP32 built as a plain repeater). Such a node has no MQTT. It takes your
signed commands over the mesh alone, from your companion radio or
through a relay. Its version has rc or arrc and no "-observer".

Set it up
  1. Flash the rc or arrc image for the board. (Wio-E5 mini has no arrc
     image: it does not fit. ar and rc do.)
  2. On its console, give it your public key and turn commands on:
       set cmd.pubkey <your 64-hex public key>
       set cmd on
     "get cmd" then says "mesh only". The first key can also come from
     a remote admin login; see [[signing]].
  3. Add it by its own public key, all 64 hex characters ("get
     public.key" on its console shows it). It is never discovered: a
     mesh-only node sends no alive message (see [[discover]]).
       mccontrol add cabin <64 hex>
     Give it no region. In the web app: Add nodes, "Add a node by its
     public key".
  4. Send the first command over the mesh, by name:
       mccontrol send cabin ver --via relay:loutest
       mccontrol send cabin ver --via mesh
     The answer carries the version, and from it the tool knows the
     node is mesh only. Until then the web app's node settings have
     "Mesh only: Yes" for a node whose version is not known.

Reach it
  Through a relay: an Observer node of yours on MQTT, with the same
  command key, that the node hears. No companion needed. See [[relay]].
  Through your companion radio: --via mesh (the web app: Mesh). See
  [[mesh]] for the companion's setting.
  Over MQTT it cannot be reached. Once the tool knows the node is mesh
  only it says so before signing, and --via auto takes the mesh.

What is different on a mesh-only node
  The mesh road is always open while "set cmd on": there is no
  cmd.mesh setting.
  It refuses what only an uplink means, as not-allowed: set wifi.ssid,
  set wifi.pwd, set cmd on <host>, ota check, ota update, cmd ping and
  the broker slots' settings (set mqttN.*).
  It has no clock source. A clock that fell behind makes it refuse
  every command; "time now" mends it (see [[mesh]]).
  It answers on an airtime budget, and a command over the budget gets
  no answer at all (see [[mesh]], "No answer").
  It shows no online or offline state: that comes from the alive
  message. "get stats" and "get sensors" still answer over the mesh.
  It is updated by USB or Bluetooth as before. There is no update over
  the mesh.

Related: [[relay]], [[mesh]], [[signing]], [[devices]].

ownregion.title: Your own command server
ownregion.body:
This is for nodes on lou-19 and older. From lou-20 every node uses the
shared command server, with no region and no IATA in its topics.

Every region can use the shared command server, mqtt-meshcore.louie.se. It serves
every IATA: keys register there, commands fan out there, and each
region's nodes are told apart by the IATA in their topics. A region can
also run its own command server (mcbroker's DEPLOY.md is the guide). Either way
it is the same tool and the same key.

Two roles

  The region operator runs the region's own command server, or chooses to
  use the shared one. On their own command server they keep the host, the certificate,
  the reader accounts for maps and Beacon, and the revoked and approved
  key files. They tell the region the command server's host name.

  A repeater owner makes a key, registers it with the region's command server,
  provisions their own repeaters over serial and adds them here. An
  owner commands only the repeaters that hold their public key; no
  operator can command someone else's repeater.

1. Make a key, once:

  mccontrol keygen

2. Point the region at its own command server. Skip this for the shared one,
which is the default:

  mccontrol config --region-broker VGR=mqtt.meshcore-vgr.se

A region with no entry uses the shared command server ("mccontrol
config --broker" changes that one). "VGR=" with no host moves the region
back to the shared one. Your devices keep their region either way, so
moving a region loses no device.

lou-20 and later: the tool talks to one command server at a time, the
shared one unless "mccontrol config --broker <host>" says otherwise; the
region table above is for lou-19 and older. Nodes set with "set cmd on
<host>" are found and reached only while that host is the tool's.

3. Register your key with each command server in use, once per server:

  mccontrol register              (every command server in use)
  mccontrol register --region VGR (that region's own server only)
  mccontrol test --region VGR     (connect, sign in, publish, receive)

4. Provision each repeater over its serial console:

  set cmd.pubkey <your 64-hex public key>   ("mccontrol key")

then the command slot. For the shared command server:

  set cmd on

For your own command server:

  set cmd on mqtt.meshcore-vgr.se

Those are the names on lou-20 or later. On lou-19 and older type
"set mqtt.cmd.pubkey", "set mqtt.cmd on" and (lou-18 and later)
"set mqtt.cmd on <host>".

On lou-17 and older, use a custom slot (here slot 3; any free one from 2 to 6):

  set mqtt3.preset custom
  set mqtt3.server mqtts://mqtt.meshcore-vgr.se:8883
  set mqtt3.audience mqtt.meshcore-vgr.se
  set mqtt3.filter all
  set mqtt.cmd.slot 3
  set mqtt.cmd on

Then reboot. The node's region comes from "set mqtt.iata VGR". It must
match the region you give the device here.

5. Add the devices:

  mccontrol discover VGR --add    (every node in VGR that holds your key)
  mccontrol add <name> <node> VGR (or one by hand)

Each device shows the command server it is reached through. Discovery
and broadcasts go to the region's command server and hear only that
region's topics, so several regions can share one server.

See [[broker]] for the command servers and [[signing]] for the key.

Back to [[index]].

protocol.title: The envelope
protocol.body:
lou-20 and later (mcc3): a command is sealed to one node and published on
mcc/cmd/<KEY>, its whole key; no IATA, no region, no broadcast. It is
encrypted (ChaCha20-Poly1305, a key from X25519 of the node's key and
yours) and signed inside by your key over the node's key, the road (MQTT
or mesh), a counter, the expiry and a reply id. The result comes back
sealed to you on mcc/r/<reply id>, a topic drawn for each session and
named only inside the command. Each node keeps a sealed alive message on
mcc/alive/<KEY> that only your key opens. The broker login is a
throwaway key per session. Over the mesh the same signed command travels
as a sealed request to the node, and its answer is sealed to you. A
command through a relay is that mesh request wrapped in a forward,
sealed to the relay on the relay's own mcc/cmd/<KEY>; the relay cannot
read what it carries. mccontrol-spec's wire format has the bytes.

A lou-20 node with an IATA code also accepts the old scheme below, until
lou-21 (see [[lou20]]).

lou-19 and older, the old scheme:

  topic    meshcore/<IATA>/<node>/cmd      one node (first 8 hex of its key)
           meshcore/<IATA>/all/cmd         every node in the region (no
                                           longer used by mccontrol)
  payload  v1|<counter>|<expiry>|<command>|<128-hex Ed25519 signature>
  signed   "<topic>" newline "v1|<counter>|<expiry>|<command>"
  result   r1|<counter>|<code>|<command>|<reply>  on meshcore/<IATA>/<node>/res

The topic is inside the signature, so a command captured from one node
cannot be replayed at another, nor a per-node command replayed as a
broadcast. The counter must be greater than the last one the node
accepted; unix seconds do that without bookkeeping. The expiry bounds a
delayed replay. A node publishes a result only when the signature
verified, so an answer of any kind proves the node holds your key.

See [[signing]], [[assurance]] and [[broker]].

reads.title: Facts: what is known about a repeater
reads.body:
What a device has told you is parsed into its settings, each with the age
of the answer that carried it: name and firmware ("get name", "ver"), tx,
rx and direct tx delay ("get txdelay" ...), autoreply and its hops, mode,
channel, private, slots or delay ("get autoreply" gives six at once), the
region map ("region"), and every other "get <setting>" by its name. A
write teaches as much as a read: "set txdelay 0.7" answered OK makes the
tx delay 0.7, as of then.

The newest answer wins. A refusal or silence teaches nothing and clears
nothing, so an old value stays with its age showing how old it is. An
answer whose signature failed (BAD SIGNATURE) teaches nothing at all; an
unsigned one, from firmware older than ar-11, still counts and is marked
unsigned. A read that is not parsed (neighbors, board, memory, the
"stats (Beacon)" line) is listed after the facts, raw, under its command.

Nothing is sent to show them: they come from what is kept on this machine,
the last answer to each read and the history of every command, and they
change the moment a result lands. Any line can be read again. The API has
them as "GET /devices/{ref}/facts"; on the command line, "mccontrol reads
<device>" prints the last answer to each read.

See [[commandlist]], [[history]] and [[stats]].

relay.title: Through a relay
relay.body:
From lou-20 a node of yours that is on MQTT can send a command by radio
to a node that is not: a mesh-only node (see [[meshonly]]), or one whose
Wi-Fi or broker has failed (see [[mesh]]). You need no companion radio.
The node that sends is the relay; the node the command is for is the
target.

  mccontrol send cabin ver --via relay:loutest

What can be a relay
  An Observer image with remote control (rc or arrc) on lou-20 or later,
  on MQTT, holding the SAME command key as the target, and in radio
  reach of it, directly or over the mesh. A relay serves the holder of
  its own command key and nobody else. A node without a command key
  never relays, and a mesh-only node cannot: it has no MQTT.

What the relay does
  It sends the mesh request the tool built for the target, waits up to
  two minutes, and returns the target's answer over MQTT. It runs
  nothing itself and cannot read the request or the answer: both are
  sealed between the target and you.

The route
  direct      one transmission, no hops: right when the target hears
              the relay itself. The default.
  --path A1B2 direct along the hops you give ("2:A1B2C3D4" for two-byte
              hashes, "--path none" for no hops again).
  --route flood       a flood in the relay's region home.
  --route flood-wide  a flood in the relay's default scope, which is
                      wider.
  An answer teaches the path. The next direct send through that relay
  uses it. A flood costs every repeater that hears it airtime, so flood
  once to learn the way, then send direct.

One command at a time
  A relay holds one command until its answer comes, or two minutes. A
  second one sent meanwhile is answered busy, or dropped unanswered if
  the two arrive together; the first goes through. Send one and wait
  for its answer. One node at a time: never a region, a county
  or a group.

The relay's budget
  Airtime: 5 % of 15 minutes (45 s on the air, about 26 commands), then
  1 % of the next 15 minutes (9 s, about 5), then a burst again.
  Floods: one a minute in a burst, one in five minutes after it, 100 a
  day, and two an hour for floods that leave the relay's region home.
  The budget is fixed. A restart of the relay opens a new burst.
  "get relay" sent to the relay shows what is left:
    > own, forwarded 3, answered 2, refused 1, burst, 39.9 s airtime
    left, floods today 1 of 100

What comes back
  The target's answer, with how well the relay heard it. Or one word
  from the relay:
    no answer     sent, nothing came back. Not a refusal: the target
                  may have run the command. See [[mesh]], "No answer".
    rate-limited  the relay's budget is used up. Wait a few minutes.
    busy          another command was waiting on the relay.
    off           relaying is switched off on the relay.
    clock-unset   the relay has no clock yet.
    expired, replay, bad-body, send-failed   nothing was sent.
  With every word but "no answer", nothing went on the air.

Switch relaying
  It is on by default. "set relay off" stops a node relaying, "set
  relay own" turns it on again. Both travel over the plane, so no visit
  is needed.

Who picks the relay
  On the command line you name the relay; --via auto never takes one.
  The web app's Auto may take a relay that hears the target directly,
  when no companion is connected, and never by a flood.

History keeps the relay, the route, how the command was sent and how
well the relay heard the answer (see [[history]]).

Related: [[mesh]], [[meshonly]], [[send]], [[cli]].

screen.title: What an interface shows
screen.body:
Every interface shows the same things, laid out its own way.

The device directory: one row per repeater you manage, with its name,
node id, region, when you last sent to it, its battery and last-seen age
once asked for, its firmware version and what it last answered. One row
is the current device. Rows can be tagged, one at a time, inverted, or a
whole region at once; a verb acts on the tagged devices, or on the
current one when none is tagged. The count of tags is always shown.

The current device's history, newest first (see [[history]]), and what it
last answered to each read, with its age (see [[reads]]). After a send,
each device's result; after a discovery, what answered.

Batt and Seen come from Beacon when you ask; see [[stats]].

A name ending in " ?" marks a device something was sent to and nothing
heard from for seven days -- no result over the control plane and no
status seen by Beacon. It is a device to look at, not a verdict: the
control plane may be off, or the node may answer another key now. A
device never sent to carries no mark, since nothing is known. Nothing
refreshes by itself; statistics, Batt/Seen and names are read when you
ask.

Every wait -- a send, a discovery, a set, a read from Beacon -- shows what
is happening and the running count, and can be stopped early; what has
come is kept.

On a narrow terminal not every column fits: the directory columns are
chosen from Reg, Sent, Batt, Seen, Ver and Result, after the name and
node ("mccontrol config --columns ver,result" does the same).

See [[keys]] for the keys, [[send]] for sending, [[discover]] for finding
repeaters.

send.title: Sending a command
send.body:
A send goes to the tagged devices, or to the current device when nothing
is tagged. Each device gets its own signed publish; the results are shown
as they come back, one line per device, with how many answered.

There is no broadcast. A send to a region (or, from the command line, to
a county with --county) sends each of your devices there its own
command, one after another in random order, spaced 10-90 s apart (5-30
min for a restart). A command that transmits on the air (a "trigger")
cannot be sent to a region; send it to one device.

A node on lou-20 or later gets a sealed command on its own topic, with no
region; one on lou-19 or older the old per-node scheme on its region.
The device view says which.

Commands that take something away ask first; see [[cautions]]. For what a
repeater admits, see [[commands]]. A refusal is explained in words:
"refused: not-allowed" means the firmware does not admit that command;
"rate-limited" means the node's budget is used up (50 commands an hour
from lou-20, 10 before), so wait a few minutes; "sig-invalid" means the
node holds a different public key than yours (see [[signing]]);
"expiry-too-far" means the node's clock is behind (see [[mesh]], "time
now").

The roads. A command goes over MQTT unless you say otherwise. A node off
MQTT is reached over the mesh, through your companion radio ([[mesh]])
or through a relay, a node of yours on MQTT that sends it by radio
([[relay]]). A node without Wi-Fi is reached only that way
([[meshonly]]). Over the mesh, no answer is not a refusal; [[mesh]]
says what it can mean.

Related: [[history]], [[protocol]], [[lou20]].

sets.title: Command sets
sets.body:
A set is a named list of commands sent in order to one device, the
tagged ones, or each of your devices in a region. Each step waits for its answer;
a refusal or silence stops the rest, so a rollout never half-applies.
Every step is recorded in history like a sent command.

The set shipped as the example, add-scope:

  1. region put {arg} *
  2. region allowf {arg}
  3. region save
  4. region

"{arg}" is asked for when the set runs (here the scope's name, such as
se-jkp). A set has six steps at most. Where sets are run, defined,
changed and removed in your interface is in [[keys]]; on the command
line:

  mccontrol sets                                   list them
  mccontrol sets --set reads ver "get name"        define one
  mccontrol sets --remove reads
  mccontrol run add-scope loutest se-jkp           run one
  mccontrol run add-scope JKG se-jkp --all         each device in JKG

A step that takes something away (see [[cautions]]) is confirmed before
the set starts, not in the middle of it.

See [[send]], [[shortcuts]] and [[commands]].

shortcuts.title: Shortcuts: nine commands on a key each
shortcuts.body:
A command per slot, sent to the tagged devices (or the current one)
without asking for the command. The result is shown and kept in history
exactly as a sent command is, and a command that takes something away
still asks first.

The slots as shipped:

  1  region          4  get autoreply
  2  ver             5  get radio
  3  get name        6  get repeat

Where the nine slots are edited, and the key each is on, in your
interface is in [[keys]]. On the command line the same slots are

  mccontrol shortcuts                 list them
  mccontrol shortcuts --set 7 "get flood.max"
  mccontrol alt 2 loutest             send slot 2's command to loutest
  mccontrol alt 1 JKG --all           to every node in a region

See [[send]], [[keys]] and [[commands]].

signing.title: Your signing key
signing.body:
Every command is signed with an Ed25519 key kept on this machine
(key.seed in the configuration directory, readable only by you). A
repeater accepts commands signed by exactly one public key, the one
given to it over its serial console:

  set cmd.pubkey <your 64-hex public key>
  set cmd on

Those are the names on lou-20 or later; on lou-19 and older type
"set mqtt.cmd.pubkey" and "set mqtt.cmd on". The second line does
the rest: with no slot configured the node takes its first free MQTT
slot (3-6), points it at the default broker mqtt-meshcore.louie.se with the
built-in "mccontrol" preset, and says "reboot to apply". A board without
PSRAM runs two slots at once; if both are its analyzer uplinks, the node
says so and asks you to turn one off (set mqtt2.preset none) -- it never
does that for you. A region's own command broker takes "set cmd on
<host>" instead; [[ownregion]] has the lines. A board without Wi-Fi
takes the same two lines and answers "mesh only" to "get cmd"; see
[[meshonly]].

The first key without a cable (lou-20)
  A remote admin, logged in to the node over the mesh with its admin
  password, may type "set cmd.pubkey <key>" too, so a board on a mast
  needs no climb. Only the first key: replacing or clearing one stays
  on the USB console. The node refuses while its admin password is the
  default, is shorter than 8 characters, or is the same as the guest
  password, and says which. This tool does not log in as an admin; use
  the MeshCore app's remote management.

Replacing the key
  Each interface shows the two lines above, creates a key when there
  is none, imports an existing seed, and replaces the key -- which
  silences every repeater provisioned with the old one. Where this is
  in your interface is in [[keys]]. Move the nodes first:
  From lou-20, "rekey <new public key>", signed by the key in use, on
  MQTT or the mesh. The new key waits on the node for 60 minutes, or
  until it restarts. It takes over the moment a command arrives that
  the new key signed; if none comes, it is forgotten and nothing has
  changed. So a mistyped or lost key does no harm.
    python -m mccontrol.rekey start     make the next key; sends nothing
    python -m mccontrol.rekey send <node> --via relay:<relay>
                                        nodes behind a relay first
    python -m mccontrol.rekey send --all   then every node on MQTT
    python -m mccontrol.rekey status
    python -m mccontrol.rekey finish    the next key becomes yours
  A node that did not answer keeps the key in use; run send for it
  again within the hour. "abort" forgets the next key while no node has
  taken it. The web app has no rekey of its own yet: rotate here, then
  move the key there with a backup file.
  A node on lou-19 or older, and a key you no longer hold, need the new
  key on the USB console.

The seed is never shown and never leaves the machine inside anything but
a signature. "refused: sig-invalid" from a node means it holds a
different public key than this one.

The same key signs you in to the default broker (see [[broker]]).
Registering it (beside the key in each interface, or "mccontrol
register") publishes your public key to the broker once, signed by the
key itself; from then on the broker checks every command against the
registered keys before it reaches any node, and a login that keeps
sending badly signed commands is locked out for 48 hours after five in a
day. Register once per key and broker, never per device: with a region
on its own broker, registering covers every broker in use.

See [[protocol]] for what the signature covers.

stats.title: Statistics
stats.body:
A device's statistics are what the fleet knows about it: battery,
uptime, noise floor, transmit and receive airtime, packets, errors and
free heap -- the block every Observer node publishes with its status --
and the last 24 hours of it in six-hour steps, or the last 48 hours, or
the last 7 days.

Where it comes from. First the node itself: one signed "get stats" (one
of the node's command slots this hour), and a node on the firmware of
2026-10-08 or later answers its counters at that moment, shown as "live,
just now" at the top; older firmware answers not-allowed and the view
says so. Then a Beacon server -- an open-source MeshCore observation
service that ingests the MQTT brokers and serves a read-only API with no
credentials. The default is beacon.meshcore-jkp.se, which covers Sweden; the
configuration has the URL for another region's Beacon, and so does

  mccontrol config --beacon-url https://beacon.example/api/v1
  mccontrol stats loutest [--live] [--range 24h|48h|168h] [--interval 1h|6h|24h]

Refreshing Batt and Seen fills the directory's columns -- battery in
volts and the age of the node's last status -- for the tagged devices,
or all of them when none is tagged, from the same source; they stay
blank until asked for and never refresh by themselves. On the command
line, "mccontrol fleet" prints the table.

The first line is always the sample's age. A sample Beacon holds is as
old as the node's last status publish (every mqtt.interval minutes),
and when Beacon cannot be reached the view says so and shows no number
at all, never a stale one as current. Nothing here sends to the mesh.

See [[screen]], [[commands]] and [[broker]].
